detail.abstract: Beneficial ownership is central to fisheries governance because a vessel's registration and flag may not reveal who ultimately controls or profits from its operations. This paper undertakes a doctrinal analysis of the treatment of beneficial ownership under Ghana's Fisheries Act, 2002 (Act 625) and the Fisheries and Aquaculture Act, 2025 (Act 1146), read alongside the Ghana Shipping Act, 2003 (Act 645) and the applicable fisheries regulations. Under Act 625, the ownership criterion formed part of an integrated classificatory scheme: Section 47(1) prescribed the requirements for a local industrial or semi-industrial fishing vessel; Section 140 classified vessels falling outside that category as foreign; and Sections 61 and 63 attached licensing restrictions and criminal consequences to foreign status. Act 1146 retains beneficial ownership as a qualification in Section 58(1) and substantially strengthens disclosure, verification and updating obligations. However, Section 170 defines foreign and Ghanaian fishing vessels principally by reference to registration under Act 645, while neither the licensing conditions in section 58(2) nor the grounds for refusal in Section 64(1) expressly state the consequence of non-Ghanaian beneficial ownership. The subsidiary registration regime likewise requires the identification and screening of beneficial owners but does not impose a nationality criterion. The paper argues that Act 1146 creates a gap between transparency and legal consequence: the State may be better able to identify who controls and benefits from industrial fishing vessels, yet the effect of non-Ghanaian beneficial ownership remains uncertain. It proposes targeted amendments to clarify whether compliance with Section 58(1) is a condition of licensing or a ground for refusal.

title: The Carbon Ceiling: Climate Conditionality and the Foreclosure of African Industrialisation

detail.title: The Carbon Ceiling: Climate Conditionality and the Foreclosure of African Industrialisation
detail.abstract: Every economy that is rich today became rich by burning things. Coal built Manchester and the Ruhr; oil built Detroit and, later, Shenzhen. The carbon those economies released over two centuries is now warming the planet, and the institutions of the developed world have responded by constructing an elaborate architecture of climate finance, carbon accounting, and conditional lending aimed at preventing the rest of the world from repeating the journey. Africa, which produced almost none of the emissions now driving climate change, finds itself on the receiving end of this architecture in a particularly acute form: development finance increasingly arrives bundled with expectations about energy mix, emissions trajectories, and fossil fuel use that no currently wealthy nation was ever asked to meet at a comparable stage of its own development. This paper examines that asymmetry directly. It traces the historical emissions record, situates Africa's negligible contribution within it, and asks what it means that the continent is nonetheless being asked to bear a disproportionate share of the adjustment. It engages seriously with the 'leapfrogging' argument, the claim that Africa can skip the fossil-fuel stage entirely, and finds it more attractive in seminar rooms than in the capital-intensive reality of industrial energy demand. It also examines two instruments that frame much of this debate at the level of metrics and policy: the carbon tax, as both a domestic and an increasingly transnational instrument through mechanisms like carbon border adjustments, and the ecological footprint concept, which measures consumption rather than production and tells an uncomfortable story about who is actually responsible for planetary overshoot. The paper does not argue that climate change is unreal, nor that Africa should be exempt from environmental responsibility. It argues something more specific: that the current architecture of climate conditionality, whatever its declared rationale, functions as a ceiling on African industrial ambition, and that African policymakers, scholars, and negotiators need a vocabulary for naming this ceiling precisely, so that the continent's energy future is decided through negotiation rather than through quiet acquiescence to terms it had no part in writing.

detail.abstract: This research aimed to evaluate the role of taxation as a complementary climate financing instrument to bolster climate mitigation and adaptation efforts in the Zimbabwean context. The study employed a critical documentary review, analysing academic journals, legislative frameworks, international reports, and other publications on climate financing. Documentary sources were complemented by insights from interviews done with key informants in the environment and climate sector. The research findings revealed that Zimbabwe has been implementing carbon taxation over the years, but its effectiveness in driving significant emissions reductions and funding targeted climate interventions has remained very limited. Specifically, there are concerns regarding its limited scope, integration into the consolidated revenue fund, and fundamental questions about its efficacy in achieving national climate goals. Overall, the study observed volatility in climate-related revenue streams on the one hand and discrepancies between policy mandates and actual fiscal allocations to finance climate action on the other. With these observations, the study recommends that the government formulate a comprehensive national climate finance policy, supported by an enabling act of parliament, to link tax systems to climate resilience explicitly. Such a policy should be expected to mandate the strategic allocation of carbon tax and other climate-related revenues to dedicated climate funds in a transparent and accountable manner. Furthermore, there should be clear, measurable targets for climate resilience, coupled with strict monitoring and oversight of tax resource utilisation to maximise the effectiveness of financial resources in strengthening Zimbabwe's capacity for climate action.

detail.abstract:
Background: Dengue transmission in the Amazon is shaped by environmental suitability, structural living conditions, and health-system response. We developed a geospatial framework to characterise dengue vulnerability and adaptive capacity as distinct but complementary dimensions in Loreto, Peru.

Methods: We conducted an ecological geospatial multicriteria analysis across Loreto. Climatic, environmental, sociodemographic, infrastructural, surveillance, and health-system indicators were harmonised to a 200 m × 200 m grid. Indicators were weighted using the Analytic Hierarchy Process informed by expert elicitation and aggregated through weighted linear combination. Monthly vulnerability surfaces were estimated from January 2014 to December 2022, and adaptive capacity was modelled separately.

Findings: We generated 108 monthly vulnerability surfaces and one adaptive capacity surface. Vulnerability ranged from 0·00 to 0·82 and clustered persistently in urban centres and along major river corridors. The highest-vulnerability quintile represented 20% of the analysed territory but contained 868 693 of 1 074 354 inhabitants (80·9%). Adaptive capacity was concentrated in Iquitos and other urban centres and was substantially lower in remote and riverine territories. Sensitivity analyses showed spatial correlations above 0·85 across weighting scenarios, with 71% of high-vulnerability hotspots consistently identified. Validation against dengue occurrence yielded an AUC of 0·60 (95% CI 0·53–0·66).

Interpretation: Separating structural vulnerability from adaptive capacity provides a more actionable basis for territorial prioritisation than composite risk measures and can support targeted, equity-oriented, and anticipatory dengue control in resource-constrained Amazonian settings.

detail.abstract: Machine learning has rapidly advanced from early theoretical concepts to a practical technology that drives many modern applications (computer vision, natural language processing, etc.). We present a detailed survey covering ML foundations, algorithmic methodologies, and empirical evaluation. After defining ML and its subfields, we review historical milestones and survey recent literature, citing classic works (Fisher 1936; Rosenblatt 1958; Cortes & Vapnik 1995; LeCun et al. 2015) and modern treatments. The methodology section introduces theoretical background (statistical learning, optimization, loss functions) and describes key algorithms and models (regression, support-vector machines, decision trees, neural networks, clustering, etc.), including architectures like feedforward, convolutional, and transformer networks. We propose a generic ML workflow (Figure 4) using flowcharts. Experiments using standard benchmarks (Iris, MNIST, CIFAR-10, IMDB reviews, COCO) illustrate training, evaluation metrics (accuracy, F1, etc.), and dataset characteristics (Table 3). Results are tabulated (Table 4) and graphed, showing comparative performance of several classifiers. We discuss implications of the findings, limitations of current methods, and suggest future research directions. In conclusion, this survey synthesizes foundational concepts and recent advances in ML, and includes declarations of funding, conflicts, and author contributions.

H4 was contrary to the expectation, and Economic Constraint was positively correlated rather than negatively. In short, all of the above results show that UKM students' choices for MacBooks are not driven by price or brand. detail.abstract: The EU has introduced an extensive ESG disclosure regime aimed at redirecting private capital to support the transition to a sustainable economy. Yet, it remains unclear whether these disclosure obligations lead to measurable shifts in the allocation and cost of capital to green firms or investments. This review aims to address this gap by developing a conceptual framework that identifies the mechanisms through which both voluntary and mandatory disclosures may influence the allocation and cost of private capital, and by systematically mapping the emerging empirical evidence against these channels. It draws on 99 publications from three academic databases (Scopus, Web of Science, EconLit) and EU institutions, published between 2010 and 2025. The review shows that the evidence base remains emerging and fragmented, but generally points to a positive association between ESG disclosure or performance and access to finance and more favourable funding conditions. At the same time, capital markets seem to anticipate regulatory compliance costs and risks, which can increase uncertainty, and in some settings, adversely affect firms with potential implications for market functioning and capital allocation and pricing. The review further highlights implications for academics and regulators. For academics, it identifies several gaps and limitations suggests avenues for future research. For regulators, it provides cautious support for disclosure regulation, while underscoring the need for credible, usable and proportionate requirements.

title: Cultural Theory-based Monetary Valuation: a framework for sensitivity analysis or addressing specific stakeholder views
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Cultural Theory-based Monetary Valuation: a framework for sensitivity analysis or addressing specific stakeholder views
detail.abstract: In social Cost-Benefit Analyses (CBAs), authorities in many jurisdictions suggest conducting sensitivity analysis at least of key parameters (such as discount rates or the approach to value mortality impacts). Rather than varying these parameters independently, using consistent sets of parameter values appears helpful in the communication of results with decision-makers. Inspired by its application in Life Cycle Impact Assessment methodologies, this study explores the feasibility of establishing consistent parameter sets based on cultural theory and outlines a corresponding so-called Cultural Theory-based Monetary Valuation (CTMV) framework. Cultural theory classifies individuals according to their social organisation, also reflecting their attitudes and preferences. Three cultural perspectives (or ways of life) actively participating in decision making processes are distinguished. 1) The individualist can be characterised in economic terms as a market and opportunity-focused utilitarian. 2) The hierarchist adheres to a utilitarianism that is institution or expert-based. 3) The egalitarian is eco-centric and concerned about (inter- and intra-generational) equity, translating also into a risk averse attitude. Parameter sets for the first two cultural perspectives can readily be defined. This is less so for the egalitarian perspective given its critical attitude towards basic economic principles (e.g. discounting or monetary valuation of non-marketed goods). Nevertheless, defining a corresponding parameter set is suggested. The proposed CTMV framework helps conducting economic assessments (e.g. in CBA or weighting in Life Cycle Assessment, LCA) according to one specific or several perspectives.

detail.abstract: Career choice, earnings, and other key economic outcomes have been linked to gender differences in willingness to compete. This paper examines how gender stereotypes shape these differences. We conduct a meta-study of prior work and demonstrate that the wide variation in gender competition gaps can be explained by stereotypes: Men enter competitions more in traditionally male-stereotyped domains, whereas in female-stereotyped domains, the gap is smaller or even reversed. Importantly, these differences are not explained by gender gaps in performance. To explore mechanisms, we collect belief data in an elicitation experiment. We find that stereotyped beliefs about gender performance differences explain more than half of the variation in competition gaps in the literature. Next, we experimentally manipulate stereotypes through framing and informational cues about others' beliefs. Although these interventions significantly shift beliefs, the effects do not translate into changes in competitive behavior. Our findings highlight the importance of stereotypes in shaping gender gaps in competitiveness while suggesting that shifting beliefs alone is unlikely to close these gaps without deeper or longer-term interventions.

detail.abstract: Armed Criminal Groups (ACGs) have long exercised territorial control over large portions of Rio de Janeiro, engaging in varied forms of criminal governance-regulating movement (e.g., restricting access by police and public service providers), imposing curfews, and resolving disputes. While the literature suggests that this control shapes electoral outcomes through patronage and restricted competition, existing studies primarily emphasize channels that shape voters' preferences-by constraining information, structuring local political networks, and favoring candidates aligned with these groups-rather than mechanisms that operate at or immediately before the act of voting itself. Motivated by a recent decision by Rio's electoral authority to relocate polling stations from areas dominated by milícias (paramilitary groups often composed of former or off-duty police officers and involved in activities such as extortion and the control of parallel markets), this work explores an underexamined alternative: whether the physical presence of polling stations within controlled territories is sufficient to independently alter electoral behavior. Using highly granular data on ACG territorial control and electoral results from four recent elections, combined with a cross-sectional regression discontinuity design (RDD) and a difference-in-discontinuities specification (Diff-in-Disc), I examine the effect of such placement on four electoral outcomes: vote concentration, support for security-force-affiliated candidates, voter turnout, and spoiled votes-the first two of which have been commonly associated with milícia rule in the existing literature. The findings show that the placement of polling stations within these territories alone does not significantly affect electoral outcomes (the equivalence tests rule out, in most cases, effects amounting to even a fraction of what the literature attributes to territorial control and criminal governance, and-where the literature offers no benchmark-to only a small share of these outcomes' own variation across polling stations). This suggests that criminal influence operates not through direct pressures at polling sites on election day, but through established channels active during the campaign period-and even before the electoral cycle begins.

detail.abstract: This study develops a uniﬁed single-lead ECG monitoring framework in which each 10.24-s segment retains point-wise premature ventricular contraction (PVC) predictions and concurrently produces a window-level atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) label. A PVC-pretrained rhythm encoder was frozen and coupled with a lightweight 1.04-million-parameter AF adapter trained using AFDB and CinC2017 records.The method achieved an F1 score of 0.9624 and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.9922 on AFDB, an F1 score of 0.9216 and speciﬁcity of 0.9800 on a held-out CinC2017 subset, and a derived record-level AF-F1 of 0.821 ± 0.032 with a macro-F1 of 0.765 ± 0.037 on the external CPSC2021 dataset. Within annotated paroxysmal-AF episodes, the native 10.24-s output achieved a window-level recall of 0.934 ± 0.045, indicating that the lower whole-record paroxysmal recall was predominantly caused by dilution when short AF episodes were averaged with many non-AF windows. Removing the rhythm feature reduced CinC2017 F1 by 6.18 percentage points, whereas a randomly initialized frozen encoder achieved an F1 score of only 0.1575. Under the same external protocol, the proposed method exceeded the best end-to-end baseline by approximately 8.8 percentagepoints in AF-F1. These results support reusable PVC-derived rhythm representations for simultaneous short-window AF assessment and point-wise PVC monitoring.

title: Beyond the Spatial Domain: Wavelet-Augmented Deep Learning for Pneumonia Screening on Chest Radiographs

detail.title: Beyond the Spatial Domain: Wavelet-Augmented Deep Learning for Pneumonia Screening on Chest Radiographs
detail.abstract: Pneumonia is a leading cause of death worldwide, and chest radiography is the first-line imaging test in most low-resource settings. Deep learning classifiers built for this task learn spatial features almost exclusively, leaving out the frequency-domain texture that radiologists rely on when reading faint infiltrates. PneuWave-Net uses both. One branch is an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B3 that reads grayscale radiographs after contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization (CLAHE). The second decomposes the same image into four Haar sub-bands (LL, LH, HL, HH) and encodes them with a small convolutional network. Concatenation fusion maps the 1536-dimensional spatial vector and the 512-dimensional wavelet vector to a 512-dimensional representation for the classifier. We train with AdamW under three-tier learning rates, focal loss with label smoothing, dual Mixup, and progressive backbone unfreezing. On a stratified 70/15/15 split of the Kermany dataset, accuracy is 97.27% with seven-fold test-time augmentation and 97.95% for a three-model softmax ensemble, giving a macro F1 of 0.9741, AUC of 0.9923, sensitivity of 0.9860, and specificity of 0.9622. Ablations with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals separate the wavelet contribution from the spatial baseline and show that CLAHE and the Haar basis both affect the result. Generalization is weaker: sensitivity drops to 88.25% on the RSNA Pneumonia Detection Challenge. Accuracy declines gradually under Gaussian noise, blur, and shifts in contrast or brightness, and Grad-CAM maps from both branches concentrate on lung fields. Total cost stays low, at 16.9 M parameters and roughly 21 ms per image on one GPU.

detail.abstract: Rapid expansion of riparian road networks, strongly shaped by river systems, is contributing to fragmentation and ecological decline in many global cities. However, few studies have explicitly examined how these interactions vary across upstream, midstream, and downstream reaches of the river systems. This study applies a Densification-Exploration framework to analyse road network development, road-river spatial coupling and links these structural changes to riparian vegetation (Enhanced Vegetation Index) in Delhi, Kanpur, and Kolkata, representing the upstream-midstream-downstream gradients of the Ganga River Basin. At system-level, the road network expansions are similarly characterised by increasing intersection density (∼340%) but stabilising complexity (∼17%) across the three cities; whereas grid-level analysis reveal that sharp increase in complexity (∼222%) are observed near major river corridors in the three cities. The upstream Delhi is characterised by an Irregular Low Density (ILD) pattern with increasing Arterial Corridors (AC), whereas increasing emergence of Dense Urban Core (DUC) patterns was observed in both midstream Kanpur and downstream Kolkata. This coincides with correlation analysis for rivers and roads, indicating a shift from exploration-dominant to densification-dominant road-river coupling from upstream to downstream cities. Road network complexity, characterised by higher entropy and greater road-river separation, is consistently associated with negative ecological effects (EVI) across all cities (average coefficients = 0.0372, p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate that riparian planning must incorporate fine-scale river-road interactions, using grid-and corridor-level assessments to capture the localised ecological impact of road expansion. This can assist in more sustainable planning and development of road networks in urban riparian zones.

detail.title: Professional Care Costs for Patients with SARI due to COVID-19 in a Public Teaching Hospital in Brazil’s Federal District: A Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing Analysis
detail.abstract: Objectives: This study analyzed the costs associated with healthcare professionals’ care for patients with Severe Acute Respiratory Infections (SARI) due to COVID-19 at the Brasília University Hospital (HUB) during the Public Health Emergency (PHE). Methods: The Time-Driven Activity-Based Costing (TDABC) methodology was used to estimate costs based on the time and remuneration of shift-based and non-shift-based professionals, across wards and PHE phases. Sociodemographic and clinical data were extracted from electronic medical records, and a multivariate analysis was conducted to identify cost predictors. Results: The total cost of the 627 hospitalizations was R$10,391,881.31, with Phase 5 (July–December 2021) having the highest expenditures, accounting for over 50% of the total costs. The yellow ward (general ward) had the highest total costs (40.3%), followed by the red ward (intensive care unit with mechanical ventilation) and the orange ward (intensive care unit without mechanical ventilation). The median per-patient cost varied significantly between the wards. The red ward had the highest median cost (R$7,269.38; IQR R$2,849.77–15,310.70). Multivariate analysis identified age (0.6% cost increase per year), female (19% increase compared to males), patient origin (55.2% higher when referred from another hospital; 72.4% higher when transferred from another HUB sector), and length of stay (4.7–5.5% cost increase per additional day, depending on ward) as significant predictors of increased costs. Conclusions: This study reveals the complex and substantial costs associated with healthcare professionals' provision of hospital care for patients with COVID-19-related SARI during the PHE.

detail.abstract: We report a structured negative result together with the narrow positive result that survives beside it. A fivefactor composite equity screen over the Nasdaq-100, whose weights were set heuristically, is decomposed into two disjoint parameter groups: composite weights, three of whose five factors derive from an undated fundamentals snapshot, and price-derived selection gates, which are point-in-time clean. We prove that the first group is not identified in our data: a factor constant in time contributes a time-invariant column to the design matrix and cannot be separated from the intercept by any pooled estimator. Non-negative least squares on these data place 92% of fitted weight on the volatility term and return unstable zero sets that do not coincide with the contaminated factors; we report these fits as uninformative rather than as confirmation, and out-of-sample R 2 reaches-0.314. We therefore decline to tune the weights, and confirm by direct search that no re-weighting is supportable: across 69 overlapping score dates (2020-08 to 2026-05, ≈ 23 effective independent windows), with Newey-West and Hansen-Hodrick standard errors and a Romano-Wolf stepdown correction replacing the naive paired t, no perturbation to any weight attains significance; the largest effect (removing the earnings-revision factor, t NW =-2.37) has a stepdown-adjusted p = 0.156. The second group is identifiable, and a walk-forward grid search over it produced the one defensible parameter change in this study, tightening the momentum gate from +25% to +15% and raising the full-sample longshort spread from +2.67% (t = 3.20) to +4.73% (t = 4.13), with the gate value selected in 100% of walkforward folds. A second optimization pass against the updated baseline yields no further uplift (-0.09%, t =-0.15), which we interpret as convergence rather than failure. We argue the separability diagnosis-asking which parameters the data can speak to before asking what their values should be-is the transferable contribution.

detail.abstract:
Unpacking Perpetual Decentralized Exchanges examines how decentralized finance is reshaping market structures beyond access, focusing on the design of systems that balance openness, efficiency, and risk in the absence of intermediaries. It positions Perp DEXs as a critical evolution, enabling leveraged derivatives trading through non-custodial, on-chain infrastructure, and outlines their core mechanics—including liquidity models, oracle systems, funding mechanisms, liquidation frameworks, order matching, and smart contracts—across leading platforms such as dYdX, GMX, Hyperliquid, and Synthetix.

The analysis identifies structural challenges such as fragmented liquidity, oracle dependency, governance centralization, and user-level risk exposure, while evaluating emerging pathways including cross-chain liquidity aggregation, diversified oracle systems, DAO-based governance, and AI-driven optimization. The report ultimately frames Perp DEXs as a foundational layer of decentralized financial markets, where sustained progress will depend on aligning technical innovation with robust system design, resilient infrastructure, and stable market dynamics.

title: A transparent evidence integration framework for translating mechanistic in silico trials into therapeutic decisions

detail.title: A transparent evidence integration framework for translating mechanistic in silico trials into therapeutic decisions
detail.abstract: Mechanistic computational models are increasingly used to support drug development by generating multidimensional biological evidence. However, transparent methodologies capable of integrating these heterogeneous outputs into reproducible therapeutic decisions remain limited. Here, we present a general evidence integration methodology that transforms mechanistic simulation outputs into interpretable support for model-informed therapeutic prioritization. The proposed framework organizes model-derived biomarkers into biologically meaningful domains, applies explicit normalization according to biomarker directionality, and integrates complementary evidence through predefined weighting strategies while preserving complete traceability from individual biomarkers to the final prioritization outcome. As a proof of concept, the methodology was implemented using the UISS-TB mechanistic model to evaluate 30 host-directed therapeutic strategies for tuberculosis. The resulting Therapy Success Score (TSS-BIO) enabled transparent ranking of candidate interventions, decomposition of domain-specific contributions, and systems-level interpretation of therapeutic performance. Beyond the tuberculosis application presented here, the proposed evidence integration methodology provides a general framework for translating mechanistic simulation outputs into transparent and reproducible evidence supporting model-informed drug development.

detail.abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery has brought about major changes in how clinical procedures are carried out today, making it possible to perform minimally invasive operations with better precision and quicker patient recovery. Still, one of the biggest hurdles in building smarter surgical systems lies in accurately detecting surgical instruments in real time. This is a problem that affects everything from automated workflow tracking to building context-aware decision support tools. Current deep learning methods for tool detection run into trouble with things like motion blur, tools blocking each other, small differences between instrument types, and the sheer computational cost of processing high-definition endoscopic video. In this paper, we put forward STFD-Net, a new deep learning architecture meant for automatic detection of surgical instruments in robotic surgery videos. The framework runs a two-stage prediction pipeline that blends local and global temporal features using learnable weights through a (PCIM). The (FPL) and Instrument Localization Head (ILH) round out the detection pipeline. We tested STFD-Net extensively on the M2CAI2016-Tool-Locations public dataset, where it reached a mean Average Precision (mAP@0.5) of 98.58% — beating out all the compared state-of-the-art approaches, including ToolH-YOLO at 97.20%, DBH-YOLO at 96.30%, and ToolNet-X at 96.40%. Beyond the overall numbers, the model also came out on top for each of the seven individual instrument categories and posted the best Precision, Recall, and F1-score among every method we evaluated.

detail.abstract: Article V develops a pricing and national-accounting framework for autonomous productive activity A while keeping produced capital K as its carrier. It separates resource cost, bundled transaction price, marginal revenue product, shadow value, imputed value, and factor-income attribution, and organizes evidence into transaction, causal, transported-benchmark, market-value, and accounting objects. detail.abstract: Trade, climate, and industrial policy in Europe, the US, and elsewhere are increasingly converging around a shared challenge: governments want to empower markets to distinguish and reward "cleaner" products, but they lack a sufficiently rigorous method for doing so. This paper proposes the establishment of a network of at least three Emissions Accounting Boards (EABs): dedicated public authorities, one each in the EU and US and at least one servicing the rest of the world, charged with developing standards for product-level emissions accounting, supporting baseline-setting, and anchoring assurance in coordination with audit enforcement bodies. The paper provides a set of jurisdictionally neutral governance considerations -- such as balancing between technocratic independence and public accountability -- before translating these into specific proposals for the EU, US, and global contexts. On policy applications, the paper works through the example of a CBAM-type tariff, showing how the EABs' standard-setting and baseline functions can efficiently empower an emissions-based border fee. The paper also addresses anti-gaming and circumvention provisions. Beyond tariffs, the paper identifies how EABs can support national competitiveness, clean procurement, and supply-chain due-diligence policies. The paper concludes that the EU and US are natural first movers in this space, each governing a market large enough for its standards to exert global pull. That movement in either jurisdiction creates strong incentives for others to follow.

detail.abstract: A sender is read by two audiences: an agent who responds to a posterior mean and a verifier who responds to a quantile of the same posterior. When the verifier’s read is convex in beliefs it cannot be gamed and an optimal disclosure is a single accept/reject partition; Value-at-Risk is not convex, the guarantee fails, and a companion paper measures the failure by the liability the binary benchmark leaves on the table. This paper answers the same question with the order of moves rather than with curvature. If compliance is irreversible and the audit comes after it, the sender does not in effect pay the quantile she is charged: refining a cell drives its expected quantile down to that cell’s lower tail average and no further, so the two-date problem is the one-date problem with Value-at-Risk replaced by expected shortfall. The parent’s structure then returns although nothing about the verifier has changed—an optimal first-date partition is binary and no sheltering disclosure is undominated—and it returns because the compliance window closes before the audit, an assumption this paper makes and then prices. The price is not small: at maximal deterrence the complying cell has mean exactly at the target, so an agent for whom delay was still available would be indifferent between complying and waiting, and any surviving value of delay would tip her to waiting for the refinement rather than acting before it; were delay fully available, the admissible refinements would be exactly the static ones and the gain would be zero. The structural half of the result survives a partial failure of the assumption and the quantitative half does not, and the paper says which is which. What timing buys, where it buys anything, is the removal of a mean condition and not of a curvature: in the static problem the complying cell is itself read, so its own lowest tail must carry enough mean to keep it complying, and that constraint binds exactly when the quantile level exceeds one half—an identity that is free of the compliance target. At a uniform prior the gain is therefore zero at or below the median and positive above it—which is precisely the region where the companion paper’s construction stops and its open problem begins. The device of deferring disclosure until a commitment is sunk is not new; what is new is the constraint that the deferral removes, and that the coherence the parent assumed can be manufactured by a sequence.

detail.abstract: We develop a relational theory of autocracy that sheds light on both the concentration of power and elite competence in authoritarian regimes. Our theoretical framework is a dynamic agency model in which the agent in one period can attempt to become the ruler in the next, capturing the ever-present threat of military and palace coups in autocracies. Under this assumption of "contestable control rights," the ruler's decision to recruit an agent of observed competence is endogenous to the anticipated cost of deterring a coup. Three key principles emerge from our analysis: 1) Incompetent rulers earning high "natural rents" from office rule alone. 2) Autocrats generally choose righthand men who are neither too competent nor too incompetent. 3) More competent rulers are willing to recruit more competent agents.

Primary data were collected from a sample of 368 respondents (N=368) through an online questionnaire and analyzed with the help of IBM SPSS and Smart PLS. detail.abstract:
Bulgaria's healthcare system combines steadily rising public expenditure with persistent structural weaknesses: an overcapacity of hospitals and beds, low occupancy, fragmented and duplicated activity, a chronic shortage and inefficient allocation of medical staff, and pronounced inequality of geographic access. This paper argues that the binding constraint is not the level of financing but the way in which resources are structured, concentrated and governed, and it develops a model for the structural transformation of the system, grounded throughout in first-source evidence from the 2024 clinical-pathway registers of the National Health Insurance Fund (NHIF).

The proposed model reorganises care into three tiers anchored by a network of 13 regional health hubs that concentrate specialist expertise, equipment and case volume, while smaller hospitals are converted into centres for emergency care, diagnostics and stabilisation without withdrawing access to basic services. Which hospitals are transformed is decided not administratively but by an objective, five-criterion scoring model adjusted for the Case Mix Index. Access is protected by an emergency system — a ground network of emergency medical aid centres and air ambulance (HEMS) — designed to bring over 95% of the population within 60 minutes of definitive hospital care. A new remuneration model links pay to workload, activity and measured medical results, with increases of up to 100% for critical staff categories, and pay-for-performance is introduced only after a Diagnosis-Related-Group tariff base is established.

Methodologically, the paper contributes an integrated financial and economic analysis: separate CAPEX and OPEX modelling, break-even arithmetic, a net-operating-transfer calculation, a value-of-a-statistical-life cost-benefit analysis, an isochrone analysis of 60-minute access, and a regional-variability analysis of induced demand. Drawing on 2,315,756 clinical pathways reported by 392 establishments, the model estimates a narrow structural saving effect of EUR 350–550 million annually, while total mature annual savings reach EUR 541–1,130 million across scenarios. The investment requirement is approximately EUR 700 million in the conservative planning case (EUR 560 and EUR 430 million under lower unit-cost scenarios), up to 86% EU-financed; it reaches cumulative break-even within four to five years under the conservative scenario, leaving a residual operating transfer of 0.4–0.6% of the state budget at maturity.

detail.abstract: Financial technology has rapidly expanded retail investors' access to securities markets, yet broader access has not been accompanied by equally rapid convergence in investment wealth. Using the 2018, 2021, and 2024 waves of the FINRA National Financial Capability Study Investor Survey, we find that mobile-app investing rose from 30.7 percent of investors in 2018 to 46.8 percent in 2024. App investors nevertheless remain substantially lower in the nonretirement portfolio-wealth distribution than non-app investors, and we find no statistically detectable convergence in that gap through 2024. Lower portfolio wealth strongly predicts mobile-app use, consistent with disproportionate adoption by investors with smaller existing portfolios. Investment-tenure results add a suggestive time dimension: by 2024, the adjusted wealth gap remains significant among low-and middle-tenure investors but is small and statistically insignificant among high-tenure investors. We refer to the coexistence of rapidly democratized access and persistent cross-sectional wealth differences as the democratization paradox. The tenure evidence suggests one way the paradox may arise: access can broaden quickly as lower-capital investors enter, while convergence in accumulated wealth may take considerably longer.

detail.abstract: Academic corruption poses a serious challenge to scientific progress, but we understand little about the impact of campaign-style efforts to curb it on research activities. This paper argues that anticorruption campaigns can affect the research output of universities that are direct targets of the campaign. We draw on evidence from more than 100 top universities in China during Xi Jinping's anticorruption inspections between 2013 and 2017. Using a staggered difference-indifferences event-study approach, we find a short-term chilling effect, a more than 10% decrease in paper publication of a university immediately following its inspection, while there is no effect beyond the first two years. At the same time, the inspection does not have a significant effect on withinprovince neighboring universities in terms of their publications. Mechanism analyses show that inspections are accompanied by declines in public research funding and publications per researcher, while private research funding is largely unaffected. These findings demonstrate that governance interventions outside conventional science policy can temporarily disrupt scientific production by shifting the institutional environment.

detail.abstract: When the government denies a noncitizen's visa application, can federal judges review that decision? For fifty years, the answer to that question was "sometimes." Though most visa denials were unreviewable, courts understood U.S. citizens to be entitled to certain procedural protections whenever a visa denial implicated their own fundamental liberty interests. But in Department of State v. Muñoz, decided in 2024, the Supreme Court upended that precedent, throwing into question whether the government is ever constitutionally required to justify its decision to deny a visa. This Article resolves that uncertainty for two groups: citizen parents with noncitizen children, and citizen children with noncitizen parents. Drawing on more than a century of precedent, it argues that citizen parents and children retain constitutionally protected interests in their relatives' visa adjudications. It further argues that these interests entitle the citizen parent or child to a facially legitimate and bona fide reason for the visa denial. Making these arguments has become urgent. In May 2026, the Trump administration announced a new policy directing virtually all noncitizens seeking to become permanent residents to leave the country and apply for a visa at a U.S. consulate or embassy abroad. That policy risks pushing hundreds of thousands of families each year into the reach of Muñoz, under which no citizen could challenge the government's decision to deny a visa. This Article explains why the Constitution demands more, even as the Trump administration mounts new barriers to legal migration.

detail.abstract: Accurate medical image segmentation under domain shift remains challenging when labeled data are scarce, the setting addressed by Semi-Supervised Domain Generalization (SSDG). Recent SSDG methods increasingly filter teacher pseudo-labels with an uncertainty signal—often an evidential (Dirichlet) head—or import a pre-trained foundation model, assuming a single model's own uncertainty cannot gate pseudo-labels reliably under shift. We test this on a standard, foundation-free testbed: a from-scratch UNet with Fourier augmentation, an EMA mean teacher, and SWAD, gated by either a confidence threshold or an evidential head. Across four benchmarks (Prostate, Fundus, M&Ms, BUSI) with three seeds we find, first, that evidential gating does not outperform a confidence threshold on any benchmark—including the Fundus optic cup, the nested fine-boundary target where a benefit would be most expected (Δ = +0.03 Dice, p = 0.87); adaptive, rank-based, and cross-view consistency gates also fail to beat the threshold. Second, direct measurement of the evidential signal explains why: the teacher's epistemic uncertainty ranks pixel error reasonably in aggregate (AUROC ≈ 0.87) but its dynamic range collapses to ∼10⁻⁴, and the ranking itself falls to near-chance (AUROC 0.64) at object boundaries, where errors live. The entire foundation-free shortfall is confined to this thin band—correcting it alone adds ∼10 Dice and closes the hardest-vendor gap to a foundation-assisted reference. Third, the hardest vendor is not explained by spectral coverage but by pseudo-label miscalibration. The practical recommendation is to use a confidence threshold by default; progress requires uncertainty signals with usable dynamic range, not just good ranking.

detail.abstract: Understanding whether the history of one variable provides genuine early warning of an impending critical transition is fundamental to clinical monitoring, financial risk detection, and ecological forecasting. In many real-world settings, the practically important question is not whether two variables are statistically dependent on average, but whether, among systems still at risk, the source history changes the predictive distribution of a critical event before it occurs. This paper develops the continuous-time event-specific branch of the Predictive-Directional Association framework. The event indicator equals one if a critical transition occurs within a prediction horizon. Event-Specific PDA compares the conditional distribution of this event indicator when the source history is available against the conditional distribution when only the target history is available, restricted to the at-risk population. We give finitestate plug-in estimators and prove consistency under independent realizations, positive at-risk exposure, and average uniform plug-in consistency conditions. We also define an event-aligned profile that evaluates the predictive contrast at fixed lead times before observed critical events. Importantly, the event indicator defines the prediction target but is not used to select or condition the training observations on future event occurrence, thereby avoiding outcome leakage. Standard Granger-type tests aggregate predictive evidence over the available time series, whereas Event-Specific PDA explicitly restricts the analysis to the at-risk set and to pre-event prediction windows. Thus Granger asks whether the past improves prediction on average, whereas Event-Specific PDA asks whether the source provides additional warning before a critical transition. The two perspectives are complementary. In particular, the present work addresses pre-event prediction, while the post-detection inference framework of Wu addresses estimation after a change has been detected. Together they cover the pre-event and post-event phases of the same critical transition problem.

detail.abstract: AI governance has primarily asked whether artificial intelligence systems are adequately governed. A less examined but increasingly consequential question is whether the expectations, demands, and authority that humans and organisations place on these systems are themselves adequately governed. This paper develops Demand-Side AI Governance as a conceptual framework for addressing this overlooked dimension. It distinguishes supply-side governance, concerned with the capabilities, design, deployment, behaviour, and control of AI systems, from demandside governance, concerned with the expectations placed on those capabilities, the decisions delegated to them, and the authority granted to their outputs. The framework identifies three interconnected objects of demand-side governance: expectation, delegation, and authority and theorises how available AI capability can be translated into progressively consequential organisational roles. A supply-demand governance matrix further identifies four configurations: Governance Alignment, Authority Inflation, Capability Vulnerability, and Compound Governance Failure. Of particular theoretical significance is Authority Inflation, in which an AI system may be technically and procedurally well governed while the organisational authority assigned to it exceeds what those controls justify. To translate the framework into organisational practice, the paper proposes three complementary mechanisms: Expectation Review, Delegation Control, and Authority Assurance. The paper argues that effective AI governance requires dual alignment between responsible provision of AI capabilities and the proportional expectations, delegation, and authority established around them. AI governance is incomplete when it governs the supply of algorithmic capability without also governing the demand for algorithmic authority.

protection, and gives an economic definition of rights: the institutional precondition
that enables an individual to enter voluntary transactions, express true preferences,
refuse coerced arrangements, and thereby form price signals. Against the tradition that
reads rights as entitlement, this definition places rights on the formation of signals;
against the existing demand-side aggregation tradition, what the paper supplies is the
precondition that tradition takes as given—pricing standards and transaction costs
determine whether a transaction can be concluded at all.

The central proposition is: one person's enjoyment is another person's employment
opportunity. When "the right to play" is protected and society possesses effective
pricing standards, "play" is the economic mechanism that converts subjective enjoyment
into the income, the employment, and the deepening division of labor of others. The
proposition is written as a payment–income duality: each item of discretionary
expenditure is simultaneously the payer's cost of enjoyment and the provider's earned
income; where a transaction is intermediated, an extraction term accruing to a third
party must first be deducted, so the scale of the expenditure flow is insufficient to
determine improvement and the destination of the flow must also be asked.

The paper examines the mutual provision of services within a single group and
distinguishes the recycling rate from participation breadth. Institutional conditions
are separated into three levels: pricing-standard clarity is endogenous to transaction
density, whereas the infrastructural component of transaction costs and institutional
permission can be set exogenously; the two constitute a positive feedback with
coexisting low and high equilibria, and the low equilibrium must be prised open from the
latter two conditions.

detail.abstract: This paper integrates Policy Transfer with the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF) to compare the transfer of Kenya’s Sessional Paper No. 4 on Energy of 2004 (KE-SP4E:2004), Nigeria’s Renewable Energy Master Plan (NG-REMP), and South Africa’s White Paper on the Renewable Energy of the Republic of South Africa (SA-WPRE). It operationalises the under-investigated problem definition and plot using Freytag’s Pyramid to capture how policy narratives structure how policies travel over time. It also shows how actors construct narrative form and links it to the modalities through which transfer occurs. Methodologically, I employ the NPF to analyse 75 public documents examining policy narratives disseminated by transfer actors engaged in the policy debate between 1983 and 2014, complemented by follow-up interviews with 22 policy actors. Statistically, Kruskal–Wallis H tests with Bonferroni adjusted post hoc comparisons identify significant differences in the deployment of narrative elements across cases, while Chi-square tests examine the distribution within cases. Within this narrative architecture, KE-SP4E:2004 and NG-REMP travelled through the hierarchical relations of the World Bank (WB), driven by the modalities of lending inducement and ideationality, and narratives casting heroes, antagonists, and beneficiaries, whereas the SA-WPRE travelled through modalities of non-lending inducement and ideationality, and was shaped by narratives casting heroes, allies and beneficiaries. Moreover, across the cases, while the WB’s ideationality under intellectual leadership enabled greater domestic brokerage, inducement in KE-SP4E:2004 and NG-REMP subordinated national priorities, whereas non-lending inducement in SA-WPRE, tempered through allyship, rendering exogenous motivations relational. The beneficiary narratives across the cases, by privileging private investors signalled credibility and depoliticised contestation over policy direction. In addition, the problem definition was predominantly framed as crisis and complexity, the constituent setting was used in setting the stage and the narrative unfolded through plots of quest and rags-to-riches, culminating in morals emphasising paradigm shift and restructuring. Applying a policy transfer lens reveals that these transfer instances were motivated more by intellectual partnership than by overt pressure, offering a framework for assessing recipient agency under asymmetric power relations.

title: The Neutrality Problem: Governance Separation as a Precondition for Cross-border Payment Interoperability Working Paper

detail.title: The Neutrality Problem: Governance Separation as a Precondition for Cross-border Payment Interoperability Working Paper

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Cross-border payment interoperability is commonly diagnosed as a technical coordination problem: align application programming interfaces, harmonize messaging standards, and adoption will follow. This paper argues that the binding constraint is increasingly located elsewhere, at the level of governance rather than technology. Wallet operators and payment service providers routinely converge on shared technical standards while resisting governance authority held by any party with a commercial stake in the settlement flow it would coordinate. This paper terms this the neutrality problem and situates it within the broader platform governance literature, where the separation of rule-writing authority from profit-capture is an established, if underused, design principle. The paper uses the Bank for International Settlements' Project Nexus as a live case to show that a neutral, governanceseparated model for cross-border interoperability is technically and institutionally feasible, but that its current success is bounded by the coordinated regulatory conditions of the participating jurisdictions. The paper concludes with a boundary-condition analysis of whether such models can extend to remittance corridors that lack an equivalent coordinating bloc, and with implications for commercial orchestration platforms and multilateral policy bodies.

title: Lessons from a Computational Audit of the European Commission’s Draft Merger Guidelines

detail.abstract: The European Commission’s draft merger guidelines describe themselves as based on the case law of the Union Courts and the Commission’s decisional practice. We test that claim against every merger decision the Commission has published to date, over 8,450 cases, a companion system with over 1,000 antitrust judgments of the Union Courts, and a third corpus holding the Commission’s antitrust decisions. Most of the text passes the test. The contested provisions do not. Their citations are real, but they anchor fragments, and the frameworks assembled from those fragments appear nowhere in the record. They are policy choices, not codification. The choices themselves are legitimate; guidelines exist to announce policy. What is not legitimate is announcing policy in the voice of settled practice. That is repairable before adoption. We take the provisions in turn. For each, we say which novelty the Commission would have to acknowledge and what the missing method would have to contain.

detail.abstract: Water provisioning remains a significant challenge in South African municipalities such as the UMkhanyakude and Mopani districts, despite constitutional (Chapter 2 of the 1996 Constitution) and legislative mandates (Water Services Act 108 of 1997) that guarantee access to sufficient water. This study evaluates the effectiveness of existing policies, practices, and governance structures in addressing these issues through qualitative methods, including document analysis. Findings reveal deficiencies in resource management, accountability mechanisms, and community participation in decision-making. The study concludes that sustainable water governance requires a multi-sectoral approach integrating improved resource allocation, enhanced accountability, and meaningful community engagement. title: The Climate Haven
affiliations: Albany Law School and Albany Law School

detail.title: The Climate Haven

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract:
Climate change is driving mass displacement. Experts project that as many as 1.2 billion people could be displaced by climate impacts by 2050, and in the United States alone, more than three million Americans have already been displaced or forced to relocate by climate-related disasters. Where will displaced people go?  Most communities are not presently equipped to absorb this influx. However, a growing number of cities are positioning climate migration as an opportunity. Places such as Duluth, Minnesota; Buffalo, New York; and Cincinnati and Cleveland, Ohio, have begun branding themselves as "climate havens," places relatively insulated from the worst climate impacts and eager to welcome new residents. The concept remains largely unexamined in the scholarly literature, despite the urgent need to understand what it means to be a climate haven as climate impacts intensify.

This Article argues that climate havens hold real promise as a model for inclusionary climate adaptation, but only if that promise is intentionally built rather than haphazardly . Realizing the promise of inclusionary climate havens requires clarifying what inclusion means in practice: whether climate havens will prioritize voluntary migrants whose relative privilege affords them the choice to relocate, or instead build capacity to receive displaced persons who have the fewest resources and the least mobility. It also requires confronting the racial, social, and economic inequities already embedded in these cities’ infrastructure and governance, inequities that shape who is protected from climate risk and who is not.

Drawing on climate science, urban planning scholarship, and a case study of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the Article develops a working framework for evaluating climate-haven claims, organized around four pillars: community belonging and ownership, infrastructure capacity, governance, and ecosystem health. In doing so, it offers both a critical vocabulary for assessing existing climate-haven branding and a roadmap for planning the equitable, resilient communities that the climate era demands.

title: The Deflated-Welch Statistic: A Closed-Form, Guaranteed-Level Test for Heteroscedastic one-Way ANOVA

detail.title: The Deflated-Welch Statistic: A Closed-Form, Guaranteed-Level Test for Heteroscedastic one-Way ANOVA

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only publicly available, de-identified datasets and simulation; it involves no human or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: One-way analysis of variance asks whether several group means differ, but its F reference needs jointly Gaussian, equal-variance errors. On the right-skewed, heteroscedastic, small-sample data common in clinical work Welch's test runs materially liberal, and a shoot-out across studentized denominators, up to the Krishnamoorthy-Lu parametric bootstrap, shows none holds size at the skewed tiny-n corner. Existing fixes each surrender a property the practitioner wants: they change the estimand, are simulation-based, stay invalid at the corner, or collapse to near-zero power. We give a test that keeps the ordinary mean, a guaranteed level, a closed form, and competitive power where Welch is valid. The test, T BB , reduces the Berger-Boos supremum to a closed-form scale inflation: a min-over-means identity makes the inner problem linear in the precisions, so the worst case is a single common-variance inflation and the guaranteed test is one deflated Welch quadratic, T BB = Q obs • exp(-R), with R = 0 returning classical Welch. The radius R is a closed form of the design, from the exact polygamma cumulants of the group log-variances plus a kurtosis tail term with a finite-n confidence guard. A fixed radius holds worst-case size at or below 0.048 across the in-scope grid; a design-adaptive radius holds size on 99% of a held-out grid while recovering most of the power, with a design-only imbalance factor for unequal group sizes. The one corner T BB cannot cross is an information limit, not a correction limit, disclosed with a minimum-sample-size rule and a conservative fallback.

title: Who Concedes Their Tax Base? The Domestic Politics of Global Taxation

detail.title: Who Concedes Their Tax Base? The Domestic Politics of Global Taxation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Harvard Center for International Development.

detail.abstract: Multinational corporations (MNCs) and migrant workers earn income abroad that both home and host states can tax. To avoid double taxation, countries have signed over 4,500 bilateral tax treaties (BTTs). BTTs limit the host state's taxing right on each overlapping tax base and allow the home state to tax the remainder. Many argue that BTTs increasingly restrict host taxing rights, undermining developing countries' ability to tax MNCs and facilitating tax evasion. When and why do states accept lower host taxing rights? I argue that democracies and left-wing governments selectively concede host taxing rights to attract foreign firms' business and investment. I construct the first global dataset of BTT contents, coding 20 provisions in over 4,000 treaties to quantify these rights across tax bases. I find that democracies across the ideological spectrum, as well as left-wing nondemocracies, grant lower host taxing rights-but only on incomes and payments generated exclusively by foreign firms, not on other bases such as foreign individuals' income or domestic firms' outgoing payments. The rise of global tax evasion reflects uneven government preferences, not merely uniform pressures from the treaty regime, and the left's conventional preference for domestic taxation does not extend to global taxation.

title: From Grain to Silver: Tax Reform, Monetary Adoption, and Economic Growth in Ming China
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong Baptist University, Princeton University and Hong Kong Baptist University (HKBU)

detail.title: From Grain to Silver: Tax Reform, Monetary Adoption, and Economic Growth in Ming China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.funderStatement: No

detail.abstract: Does the adoption of money promote long-run economic growth? We study this question by exploiting the silverization of the fiscal system in Ming China (1368-1644), a reform that progressively converted taxes collected in grain into silver payments. Economic historians and contemporary Ming observers identify this fiscal transformation as the principal channel through which silver entered local economies as a medium of exchange, propagating beyond fiscal settlement into private commerce. Using the early-Ming tax structure-specifically, the share of grain tax designated for shipment to the central government-as an instrument for prefectural tax monetization, we find that a one-standard-deviation increase in the tax monetization rate generated approximately 13 additional log points of population growth between 1393 and 1580, relative to a sample mean of 88 log points. We trace the effect through three channels: market expansion as reflected in the growth of local markets and commercial routes, product specialization as measured by the emergence of commercial centers for silk, silkworm, and tea production, and enhanced state capacity through the mitigation of conflict.

title: From Near-Death Experience to Rebirth: A Continuity Model of Consciousness Across Biological Death - An Interdisciplinary Framework for Examining the Possible Relationship Between Near-Death Experiences, Reincarnation Memories, and Survival of Consciousness

detail.title: From Near-Death Experience to Rebirth: A Continuity Model of Consciousness Across Biological Death - An Interdisciplinary Framework for Examining the Possible Relationship Between Near-Death Experiences, Reincarnation Memories, and Survival of Consciousness
detail.abstract:
Near-death experiences (NDEs) and reports of memories of previous lives have traditionally been investigated as separate categories of exceptional human experience. NDE research primarily examines experiences occurring during or around episodes of severe physiological crisis, whereas reincarnation research has focused particularly on young children who spontaneously report memories apparently belonging to another deceased individual. Despite their different contexts, both phenomena raise related questions concerning memory, personal identity, subjective continuity, the relationship between brain activity and consciousness, and the possibility that some aspects of consciousness may not be completely explained by conventional models of brain-dependent cognition.

The present paper develops a Continuity of Consciousness Model (CCM) as a conceptual framework for examining a possible relationship between NDEs and reincarnation-type experiences. The model does not assume that reincarnation or post-mortem survival has been established. Instead, it proposes that the two phenomena can be investigated within a common research framework consisting of three analytically distinct phases: (1) altered consciousness associated with biological crisis, (2) a proposed transition or discontinuity between embodied states, and (3) subsequent reports of identity- or memory-related continuity.

The model is compared with competing explanations, including neurophysiological mechanisms, memory reconstruction, psychological dissociation, cultural expectation, cryptomnesia, coincidence, information transfer, and survival hypotheses. Contemporary NDE research provides evidence that conscious experiences and subsequent recall can occur in association with cardiac arrest and resuscitation, although the timing and neural basis of such experiences remain debated. The AWARE-II multicentre study, for example, reported different categories of recalled experiences among cardiac-arrest survivors while simultaneously investigating EEG and cerebral oxygenation. Contemporary neuroscience has also proposed integrated neurophysiological explanations for NDE phenomenology.

In parallel, decades of case investigations have documented children who spontaneously claim memories of previous lives, including cases in which statements were investigated against records concerning deceased individuals. A particularly relevant theoretical contribution has proposed comparisons between NDEs containing apparent past-life memories and children's reincarnation-type memories.

The present study therefore proposes a research programme rather than a metaphysical conclusion. It develops operational definitions, comparative variables, falsifiable predictions, a proposed database methodology, an evidence-grading system, and directions for prospective investigation. The central hypothesis is that if NDEs and reincarnation-type cases reflect a common underlying phenomenon, measurable phenomenological and informational correspondences should occur more frequently than would be expected from cultural, psychological, or chance explanations alone. Conversely, systematic differences would support the interpretation that the two phenomena are independent.

title: From Watchdog to Gatekeeper: A Scoping Audit of Editorial Appointments and Disclosure Gaps Among Post-Publication Scrutiny Actors
