detail.title: From Watchdog to Gatekeeper: A Scoping Audit of Editorial Appointments and Disclosure Gaps Among Post-Publication Scrutiny Actors

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial competing interests relevant to this preprint.

detail.abstract: Post-publication commenters, data sleuths, research-integrity journalists, and investigators increasingly move between public accusation, scholarly authorship, publisher employment, peer review, and journal governance. This preprint tests whether those role overlaps are publicly visible and procedurally managed. A document-based scoping audit, completed on 25 August 2026, examined a purposive cohort of twelve publicly identifiable post-publication scrutiny actors and current journal or publisher materials. Five members of the cohort had a current scholarly-journal appointment presented as an editor or editorial-board listing; one held a current distinguished-reviewer-board position that should not be misreported as an editorship; and six had no current scholarly-journal editorial appointment located. None of the five current editorial appointment pages linked a standardised individual declaration of financial and non-financial interests. Public pages also rarely specified whether ordinary board members could select reviewers, handle manuscripts, recommend decisions, access confidential submissions, or participate in post-publication cases. Detailed analysis of Ivan Oransky at Research Integrity and Peer Review, Elisabeth Bik at Stacks, and the historical use by John Carlisle of confidential submission materials for a published integrity analysis demonstrates three distinct risks: structural subject-matter overlap, continuing public investigation of potential authors or papers, and conversion of privileged editorial access into a research corpus. The audit does not establish that any named person biased a decision, misused information, or received undisclosed payment. It establishes a narrower and consequential failure: the public record is generally insufficient to test independence, reconstruct recusals, or distinguish symbolic appointments from decision-influencing authority. A rank-sensitive classification, conflict-trigger test, and minimum governance standard are proposed. Where overlap is continuous and meaningful recusal would remove an appointee from a substantial part of the journal's remit, the institution should not appoint or retain that person in a decision-influencing role unless it can demonstrate independent, auditable safeguards.

title: Impact of Macroeconomic Factors on the Performance of the Indian Stock Market: An Empirical Study Using NIFTY 50

detail.title: Impact of Macroeconomic Factors on the Performance of the Indian Stock Market: An Empirical Study Using NIFTY 50
detail.abstract: The Indian stock market has witnessed significant growth over the last decade, with increasing participation from retail investors, institutional investors, and foreign investors. During the same period, the Indian economy experienced several major events such as demonetisation, the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax, the COVID-19 pandemic, rising inflation, changes in monetary policy, and fluctuations in foreign capital flows. These developments have influenced market behaviour in different ways, making it important to examine how key macroeconomic variables affect stock market performance. This study therefore analyses the impact of selected macroeconomic factors on the performance of the NIFTY 50 index, which is considered a benchmark of the Indian equity market.

title: Catastrophic Health Risk and Retirement Portfolio Choice
affiliations: and University of Torino -Department of Economics ESOMAS

detail.title: Catastrophic Health Risk and Retirement Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract: A well-documented pattern in US household portfolio data is that the conditionalrisky share remains broadly stable throughout retirement. We ask whether rare but catastrophic health-expenditure shocks in retirement are sufficient to account for this pattern. We develop aparsimonious life-cycle portfolio-choice model in which rare health disasters,calibrated from Health and Retirement Study (HRS) evidence on severelong-term-care episodes and out-of-pocket medical spending, can absorb a largeshare of current retirement income and weaken the safe-asset role of pensionincome. Under this data-driven calibration, the model reproduces the nearlyflat risky-share profile observed in the Survey of Consumer Finances andgenerates a negative health gradient consistent with HRS panel evidence,without bequest motives, housing, annuity choice, endogenous health investment,or recursive preferences.

title: Better Information, Cheaper Capture: Personal AI and Selective Evidence

detail.title: Better Information, Cheaper Capture: Personal AI and Selective Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: I received no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Personal AI could help citizens understand complex policies by filtering relevant evidence from noise. That saves time but also lets the provider decide which facts reach the user. Users may have stable broad values without a settled view on an unfamiliar policy, while the questions an AI asks to clarify those values may themselves shape what the user comes to prefer. For this paper I hold broad values fixed and model the narrower risk from evidence selection. Because checking may require much of the work the AI was meant to save, a provider offered a reward tied to the policy outcome can omit true evidence and focus on users who are likely to change, unlikely to check, or politically influential. The same user information that improves advice can thus help the provider protect an inefficient policy at lower cost. In a preregistered audit using fixed official sources, I show that a hidden instruction to favor one side changes both the selected evidence and the recommendation, while access to the full source set improves detection. My exploratory reanalysis of public experimental data suggests that information already known about people can help identify who is most likely to change their views after assistance. I therefore propose AI verification as a public good: a service that compares and summarizes evidence from independently owned systems could lower checking costs and give providers a reputational reason to expose one another's omissions, although biases shared across systems would remain.

title: Trumpian Authoritarianism and the Future of Antitrust
affiliations: American University - Washington College of Law

detail.title: Trumpian Authoritarianism and the Future of Antitrust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Trumpian authoritarianism harms antitrust and, consequently, national prosperity, in two ways. First, direct political influence in antitrust enforcement will increasingly impede economic growth through the exercise of market power, wasteful rent-seeking, and distorted investment. Second, the authoritarian trend jeopardizes in a fundamental way the role that antitrust has played in U.S. domestic economic regulation since the mid-twentieth century. A faltering liberal democracy threatens to unwind the underpinnings of an eight-decade political settlement that reoriented domestic economic policy, including antitrust, around the pursuit of inclusive economic growth. That places further stress on antitrust institutions that are already under pressure from increased market power, growing inequality, and the possible emergence of the ultra-wealthy politically as a concentrated interest group. An unraveling of that political settlement will hamper economic growth and shared prosperity. Rebuilding U.S. antitrust institutions will require both procedural and substantive reforms. Those reforms are necessary and important but will not succeed unless they are part of a broader reconstruction of governmental institutions to restore liberal democracy.

title: Human-AI Human Cognitive Co-evolution: From Cognitive Synergy to the Recursive Development of Human and Artificial Cognitive Capability

detail.title: Human-AI Human Cognitive Co-evolution: From Cognitive Synergy to the Recursive Development of Human and Artificial Cognitive Capability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Human-AI Cognitive Co-Evolution, Human-AI Collaboration, Cognitive Development, Cognitive Outsourcing, Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, Metacognition, Human Capital, Hybrid Intelligence, Recursive Interaction, Human-AI Complementarity

Research on human-AI interaction has largely examined what humans and artificial intelligence can accomplish together. Studies increasingly document effects on productivity, task performance, decision making, learning, creativity, and professional work. A different question has received considerably less longitudinal attention: what does sustained interaction cause the participants and their cognitive relationship to become over time?

This paper develops Human-AI Cognitive Co-evolution (HACC) as a theoretical framework for examining that question. HACC concerns the recursive developmental process through which sustained interaction between human and artificial cognition can alter human cognitive capabilities, the effective cognitive contribution obtainable from artificial intelligence, the relationship through which those capabilities are combined, and the resulting joint cognitive capability of the human-AI system.

HACC extends the earlier Human-AI Cognitive Synergy formulation by shifting the unit of analysis from developmental effects principally on the human participant to reciprocal developmental dynamics within the human-AI relationship. Reciprocity does not imply symmetry. Humans develop through learning, experience, reflection, knowledge acquisition, strategy formation, neuroplastic adaptation, and changes in judgment. Artificial systems change through fundamentally different mechanisms, including model development, system configuration, context, memory, retrieval, tool integration, and changes in the capabilities that human users are able to elicit from otherwise unchanged systems.

The framework distinguishes HACC from Human-AI Cognitive Outsourcing (HACO), a trajectory in which artificial intelligence performs an increasing share of cognitive activity without corresponding development of the human capabilities necessary to perform, understand, evaluate, or meaningfully integrate that activity. HACC and HACO are not binary states. Different cognitive capabilities may simultaneously be developed, maintained, deliberately delegated, or displaced.

The paper further distinguishes local capability bounds, interaction bounds, and long-run developmental bounds. Particular human, artificial, and joint capabilities are constrained. Individual recursive episodes must also terminate when the expected value of further cognitive iteration no longer justifies its costs. These observations do not, however, establish that the developmental trajectory of a changing human-AI cognitive system must converge toward a single fixed global ceiling. HACC therefore treats long-run development as potentially open-ended rather than unbounded, leaving the existence and location of global developmental limits as empirical questions.

A dynamic model is developed to represent multidimensional human capability, base and effective artificial capability, recursive interaction, cognitive complementarity, joint capability, cognitive outsourcing, endogenous local frontiers, regime change, problem-space expansion and contraction, and bounded recursive episodes. The framework generates falsifiable propositions and identifies the longitudinal evidence required to distinguish cognitive co-evolution from augmentation, learning, adaptation, and outsourcing.

The central proposition is not that human-AI cognitive co-evolution has already been empirically demonstrated. It is that increasingly persistent interaction between human and artificial cognition creates developmental relationships that cannot be understood adequately through measures of immediate performance alone. Understanding those relationships requires examining not only what humans and AI produce together, but what capabilities they develop, preserve, reconfigure, or lose through sustained interaction.

title: China's Role in Shaping the Future of Global Arbitration
affiliations: Ohio Northern University - Pettit College of Law and East China University of Politics & Law

detail.title: China's Role in Shaping the Future of Global Arbitration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

detail.abstract: This article examines how China’s evolving arbitration system may contribute to the future development of international commercial arbitration. Rather than predicting that Chinese models will displace established approaches, it identifies several structural and institutional features that position China to influence an increasingly pluralistic global arbitral order. First, China’s emphasis on substantive justice and outcome coherence offers an alternative conception of arbitral legitimacy that places institutional responsibility and consistency alongside party autonomy and procedural fairness. Second, the scale, administrative capacity, and centralized infrastructure of Chinese arbitration institutions create distinctive advantages in digitalization, artificial intelligence, data-driven quality control, online dispute resolution, and system-wide technological innovation. Third, China’s long experience with hybrid processes such as arb-med-arb demonstrates how adjudicative and consensual dispute resolution can be integrated within institutionally supported frameworks, while also highlighting the importance of consent, role clarity, and procedural safeguards. Finally, China’s development of coordinated “one-stop” systems linking courts, arbitration, and mediation illustrates an alternative approach to dispute-resolution architecture based on institutional coordination rather than strict separation. The article argues that these developments are best understood as context-specific contributions to a polycentric international arbitration system. China’s significance therefore lies less in exporting a single model than in demonstrating that familiar arbitral values—including fairness, efficiency, autonomy, consistency, and enforceability—can be realized through different institutional configurations. As international arbitration becomes more geographically and institutionally diverse, China’s experience broadens the range of models available for comparative study, adaptation, and future innovation.

title: The Coupled Absorber Regime: Functional Monetary Failure Under an Intact Settlement Shell

detail.title: The Coupled Absorber Regime: Functional Monetary Failure Under an Intact Settlement Shell

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patient data, clinical research, or personally identifiable research subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that a monetary system can undergo functional failure while its settlement infrastructure remains operational. Payments settle, sovereign debt rolls, repo clears and auctions are covered, yet the system no longer reliably delivers the stabilizing functions associated with monetary elasticity: weak private demand does not consistently produce a durable sovereign rescue bid; lower expected policy rates do not guarantee lower long-term borrowing costs; abundant secured funding can coexist with contracting refinancing capacity; and official intervention can protect one observable by transferring cost into another constrained balance sheet.

The paper develops the coupled absorber regime. An absorber is a balance sheet, institution, market or physical buffer that receives stress generated elsewhere. The regime becomes coupled when continued operation at one impaired node depends on another constrained node accepting part of its cost. Settlement persists through financed Treasury demand, collateral and margin protection, official liquidity, constrained institutional demand, gates, extensions, reserve intervention, fiscal transfer, physical-buffer depletion and strategic non-withdrawal. These mechanisms expand displacement capacity without necessarily rebuilding restoration capacity.

The paper also clarifies the relationship between the December 2025 working map, the canonical DST framework, the post-elastic financial-systems paper and the 2026 record. The December analysis identified Triffin exhaustion, deterioration in the Treasury countercyclical rescue function, repo and collateral, Japan and trust as load-bearing nodes. Its terminal 0–72-hour liquidation mechanics were conditional on stress reaching a point where rollover, usable collateral and transfer to the next absorber failed; they were not the definition of monetary failure itself. The canonical DST framework formalized why visible stability can coexist with declining tolerance under displacement, while the post-elastic financial-systems paper applied that distinction to finance and separated state diagnosis from event timing. The subsequent record did not produce the terminal synchronized-refusal phase. It revealed the intermediate regime the framework allows: functional monetary failure under continuing settlement, sustained by increasingly coupled absorbers.

Two mechanisms sharpen the architecture. First, gross cash, margin and collateral obligations can bind before contractual netting, asset maturity or economic offsets become usable; a system can therefore be net-solvent and operationally illiquid. Second, official facilities such as BTFP and FIMA can temporarily suppress forced sale by adding a funding claim against already load-bearing collateral. The immediate price observable is stabilized while encumbrance, repurchase and rollover obligations increase.

The historical control comparison is severe: from early 2022 to 31 July 2026, gross federal debt rose from approximately $30 trillion toward $40 trillion, SOFR transaction volume rose from roughly $0.8–$0.9 trillion to $3.205 trillion, and the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 1.81 percent to 4.75 percent. The settlement shell became larger and busier while the marginal financing floor rose.

The contribution is not a forecast date. It is a mechanism: functional monetary failure can persist as a managed regime while costs move across balance sheets, currencies, recognition clocks and physical systems. The forward thesis is that voluntary, low-cost and restorative absorption is narrowing, while larger transfers increasingly require financed, constrained, depleting or cross-sovereign recipients.

title: Quotation-Form Failure Does Not Establish a Capability Limit: A Constructive Replication of Nguyen and Welch's Study of LLM-Assisted Qualitative Coding

detail.abstract: Nguyen and Welch report out-of-source quotations in their ChatGPT coding runs, discuss truncation and fabrication in comparison studies, and argue that these and related reliability problems are rooted in large language model (LLM) architecture. They also report a best-case qualitative-AI (Qual-AI) condition in which quotations matched the source while thematic connection and coverage remained weak. I test a narrower proposition: whether quotation-form failures persist when a contemporary execution configuration explicitly requires contiguous source spans. A constructive replication analyzed a 14-document candidate corpus in 252 item-level Responses API requests using dated GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.5 snapshots and GPT-5.6 Sol as served on August 11, 2026. Under the published zero-shot instruction, normalized contiguous-match rates among extracted quotation-like strings on the ten plausibly equivalent documents were 44.3%, 65.8%, and 64.4%. Under a concise exact-span configuration that prohibited editing, permitted omission, and used low reasoning effort, the corresponding conditional rates were 93.3%, 98.8%, and 95.9%. A bundled-input sensitivity, closer to the focal execution unit, produced rates of 98.9%-100%, although three of 18 responses were incomplete. A post hoc AI-assisted classification of a nonprobability diagnostic sample found that several non-verbatim strings were source-traceable and propositionally supported, while one composite created an unsupported cross-device relation. In the tested corpus, contemporary LLM configurations produced source-exact candidate quotations at high conditional rates when the evidentiary rule was explicit. Quotation-form errors observed in dated execution configurations therefore do not establish that normalized-contiguous source selection is architecturally unavailable. Models and interfaces can change within a publication cycle, but the observed ordering does not support monotonic improvement. Exactness does not establish relevance, coverage, or interpretive adequacy, and Nguyen and Welch's broader claims about qualitative analysis remain untested.

detail.abstract:
Japan's amended Act on the Promotion of Ensuring National Security through Integrated Implementation of Economic Measures, known as the Economic Security Promotion Act (ESPA), cleared the House of Councillors in June 2026. 

The amendment does five things: it widens the range of support available for securing a stable supply of specified critical materials, and so strengthens supply chains; it brings an additional industry within the critical infrastructure services regime and improves how that regime is administered; it expands the set of funds eligible to support the development of advanced technology; it extends support to overseas projects that matter for economic security; and it establishes a dedicated research organization and a public-private council for economic security. What stands out in this amendment is that the territory covered by Japan's economic security legislation has expanded from the tangible to the intangible and from domestic activities to overseas activities. 

This study examines what is new in the amended ESPA and sets out the implications for Korea's economic security policy.

detail.abstract: International science, technology and innovation cooperation has become harder to govern as geopolitical tensions, export controls, and competing approaches to technological security reshape global knowledge networks. This paper discusses the governance problem created by this shift. It argues that traditional coordination mechanisms, which often separate research policy, foreign policy, industrial development, and regional economic planning, are poorly suited to projects that require sustained collaboration from basic research through commercialization. Using a systems perspective and a review of research on international scientific collaboration, science diplomacy, and innovation policy, the paper identifies three recurring governance gaps: fragmented responsibilities across public institutions, weak links between international research projects and industrial demand, and limited capacity to evaluate results beyond publications and formal agreements. The paper proposes a practical governance framework built around cross-sector coordination, project-based planning, lifecycle-oriented evaluation, and regional participation. It also considers the role of science diplomacy in preserving professional communication and creating workable conditions for cooperation when formal interstate relations are uncertain. The central conclusion is that the effectiveness of international science and technology cooperation depends less on the number of contacts than on the institutional capacity to translate them into shared knowledge assets, skills, technologies, and economic applications.

detail.abstract:
This study analyzes the paradoxical mechanism by which one country's protectionist industrial policy unintentionally redirects the path of technological innovation in its trading partners, often to the supplying country's own disadvantage. Historical episodes, including the OPEC oil shock, the Soviet Union's threats to natural gas supplies to the West, China's rare earth embargo against Japan, and US semiconductor export controls against China, share a common pattern.

First, the supplying country restricts exports of the resources and technologies it holds, or manipulates their prices, inflicting a supply shock on the importing country. The relative price of the resource then surges, dramatically raising the incentives of firms and researchers in the importing country to develop substitute and workaround technologies. Private R&D combines with the government's directed industrial policy (R&D subsidies, public procurement, and regulatory reform) to bring substitute technologies quickly to market. Over the long run, the importing country's dependence on the resource declines, and the supplying country's bargaining power and market position erode. 

This study argues that a supply restriction strategy raises short-term bargaining power but can carry a self-defeating quality, eating away the supplier's own market base. For the importing country, by contrast, a supply shock can become the occasion for a technological leap, and here the government's directed industrial policies, R&D subsidies among them, act as complements that accelerate private innovation.

detail.abstract: We review recent research on the trio of artificial intelligence (AI) practices—electronic platforms, machine learning, and large language models—and their effects on those who use and work with them. Because these tools take over specific tasks from existing jobs, the important effects are how the remaining work changes and how workers react to it. Perhaps our main conclusion is that choices as to how they are used are the most important factor in their effects on those who use them. For example, do they take over boring tasks like note-taking or interesting ones like drafting reports? Do workers spend their saved time checking AI output or taking on new tasks? We describe the wide variety of outcomes and emerging issues such as the ability of chatbots to show empathy, the ability to codify what had been tacit human knowledge, and the development of digital twins, which predict responses from specific individuals.

detail.abstract: LLM-based AI systems are increasingly used for social simulation, but their simulated behavior may systematically diverge from real human behavior. We develop a computable framework for deciding when simulations can be used directly, when they should be corrected with human data, and when to stop recruiting humans. The Human-Debiased Estimator (HDE) uses the behavioral parameter estimated from AI simulations as a potentially biased anchor. A finite-sample bound selects the anchoring strength, adaptively choosing among AI-only, hybrid, and human-only estimation, and yields a sequentially valid stopping rule. Across 20 controlled settings and 4 real-data applications, HDE improves prediction accuracy and stability.

detail.abstract:
As AI advances, it returns something more valuable than incremental efficiency gains: time. The Gift of Time: AI, Automation, and the Future of Work in a Time-Rich Economy argues that intelligent systems are compressing workflows and reducing routine cognitive and operational burdens at scale—reshaping how work is structured and how value is created. This opinion piece examines the compression of work across sectors, shifts in employment structures, and the implications of an economy in which machines perform an increasing share of necessary tasks.

From an education perspective, it outlines two diverging futures in a time-rich society: one in which reclaimed time supports learning, creativity, and civic engagement, and another in which it is absorbed by attention-maximizing digital systems. The paper contends that leaders across education, policy, and industry must make deliberate choices about how AI-generated time is distributed and used. It proposes that governance frameworks incorporate time-based metrics alongside financial returns, and that closing the reskilling divide is essential to ensuring that the time dividend expands inclusion rather than deepening inequality. By treating time as a first-class economic and ethical variable, the paper positions AI not only as a driver of productivity but as a lever for long-term human flourishing.

detail.abstract:
This study and mini-documentary are an examination of the nonprofit industry’s political economy—the deemed “third sector” of the United States economy, who according to the Urban Institute is responsible for over three trillion dollars in revenue, over one million public charities and organizations, and employing approximately ten percent of the nation’s workforce. Due to the government’s inability to efficiently and directly address the needs of communities and the limits of available resources, the nonprofit sector is currently filling more gaps and under more pressure to improve quality of life. As a result of the political economics, valuable work in the sector is marginalized and often organizations marginalize themselves by design. My thesis is an organization’s success is dependent on its leverage of the industry’s political economics and proactive positioning within the social politics of society.

The case study is Impact Repertory Theatre, an Oscar and Grammy-nominated performing arts and leadership training grassroots program, founded in 1997 for Harlem, New York City and surrounding underserved communities. It is a query into the dynamics of its success, challenges, and a determination of what shifts in its social, political and economic structure will be needed to sustain its mission.

The methods employed for this study include research into the protocols of nonprofit organizations and institutions, the growth of the nonprofit industry in recent decades, and the parallels of for-profit laws, standards and practices. This includes the assumed characteristics of new nonprofits, strategic financial planning, “institutional readiness,” branding, marketing and public image, the role of technology, new media, mission driven transformation and cause related marketing.

These resources were supplemented by additional research in the dynamics of organizational failure, parallels in the planning and execution of family-owned for-profit businesses, and the dynamics of leadership. Internal interviews were conducted with executives, advisory board members, staff and participants of Impact Repertory Theatre. Noted external interviews were conducted with professionals and social entrepreneurs in fields including the arts, scholarly writing, philanthropy, finance, communications and business administration.

title: Observational Compression, Spectral Persistence, and Geometric Illusions: A Cross-Domain Empirical Audit of Institutional Dynamics in Monetary and Health Systems

detail.title: Observational Compression, Spectral Persistence, and Geometric Illusions: A Cross-Domain Empirical Audit of Institutional Dynamics in Monetary and Health Systems

detail.abstract: This paper develops and empirically audits a cross-domain framework for studying dynamic institutional systems when the economically meaningful state is only partially observed. The central object is an observational compression map that transforms a potentially high-dimensional institutional state into a lower-dimensional collection of recorded outcomes. The framework combines reduced-form dynamic estimation, spectral decomposition, observability analysis, Principal Component Analysis (PCA), real Schur geometry, robustness estimators, bootstrap inference, regime diagnostics, falsification tests, and strict out-of-sample forecasting. The empirical design compares two substantially different Argentine institutional environments: a high-frequency monetary system represented by Central Bank balance-sheet dynamics and a low-frequency federal health system represented by annual provincial dynamics in consultations, live births, and deaths. The comparison is deliberately non-causal across domains. Rather, the two systems form a comparative laboratory for identifying which properties of observed dynamics are robust to changes in ontology, frequency, aggregation, and measurement. The main result is methodological. Both systems can display compact spectral representations in which persistence, contemporaneous variance, and observed outcomes appear geometrically organized. However, the health application demonstrates that formal observability does not imply practical observability, that dominant variance need not coincide with dominant persistence, and that visually compelling PCA-Schur alignment can be reproduced under temporal and spatial null constructions. In the health panel, the two-way fixed-effects transition matrix has spectral radius 0.477, while Anderson-Hsiao produces a materially lower radius of 0.215; both remain locally stable, but they should not be interpreted as estimates of an unobserved "true" institutional operator. A second-order specification remains stable with companion spectral radius 0.569. The leading PCA component explains 51.9% of raw dynamic variance, but its alignment with the dominant Schur direction is only 0.563 (angle 55.7°), and the corresponding alignment is not unusual under either the within-province temporal or cross-jurisdiction spatial placebo distributions. Strict rolling forecasts further show that the full three-dimensional state does not improve upon a parsimonious death-growth benchmark. The evidence therefore supports a weaker but more general conclusion: observationally compressed institutional systems can exhibit stable reduced-form dynamics and apparently meaningful spectral geometry without providing evidence of causal transmission or structurally unique latent mechanisms. Cross-domain comparison is consequently useful not because it establishes a common causal chain, but because it exposes the inferential boundary between dynamic regularity, observability, geometry, and identification.

detail.abstract: Recent calls for reforming public health to exert greater political influence misdiagnose the field's main challenge. Public health institutions have demonstrated considerable capacity to influence policy, shape the generation and dissemination of knowledge, and invoke moral authority in support of population health goals. The COVID-19 pandemic made this influence particularly clear, but also exposed the risks of exercising influence amidst scientific uncertainty and legitimate disagreement over competing values. Public health knowledge is necessarily dynamic and fallible, and health represents one important value among many that policymakers and the public must balance. Similarly, popular assumptions within public health about individual responsibility, markets, and government intervention, warrant greater intellectual scrutiny rather than taken as settled science. Reforms focused on accumulating greater influence risks further eroding public trust if these scientific limitations and moral blind spots remain unaddressed. Public health should instead prioritize producing credible knowledge, openly acknowledging uncertainty and policy trade-offs, and incorporating greater ideological and moral pluralism. Then, and only then, can we as a field begin to rebuild institutional trust. Rather than become an objective unto itself, societal influence can be more effectively and sustainably performed from trustworthy institutions.

detail.abstract: In an appendix to Lógica Viva (1910), Carlos Vaz Ferreira records a colleague's suggestion — pensar por sistemas para tener en cuenta, to hold systems as considerations rather than commitments — and explicitly leaves its development to the reader. This paper takes up that development for one particular domain: theory selection in applied social-scientific fields such as economic development and strategy, where competing, mutually compatible theories coexist without any principle for deciding which applies to a given case. The paper argues that the missing principle is supplied by the structure of the problem itself, characterised as two states and a missing connector, with theories treated as architectures of solution valid only for the simplified state each presupposes. A single procedure both selects an architecture when one fits and reports the absence of a fitting architecture when none does — turning the unit of organisation for accumulated knowledge from theoretical tradition into problem class. The framework is distinguished from eclecticism, positivism, and constructivism, grounded in an unrepresentativist realism about problem structure, and illustrated across three domains — vaccination campaigns, industrial cluster upgrading, and WTO dispute settlement — showing how the same phenomenon admits different characterisations that select different architectures.

title: Terminal Value: What Death Was Doing for the Economy, and What Happens When We Stop It

detail.title: Terminal Value: What Death Was Doing for the Economy, and What Happens When We Stop It

detail.abstract:
Economic models treat human mortality as a boundary condition rather than a variable. This is defensible as long as the parameter does not move, and for the entire history of the discipline it has not: while life expectancy at birth has roughly doubled since 1850, the maximum human lifespan has not measurably changed. This paper argues that mortality performs at least five distinct economic functions, that none of them has an institutional substitute, and that a sustained increase in healthy lifespan would remove all five simultaneously.

The five functions are: (1) mortality supplies the hazard term in the effective discount rate, so that falling mortality mechanically compresses real rates and drives the present value of perpetual assets toward divergence; (2) inheritance constitutes the largest recurring redistribution in a market economy, interrupting the compounding that would otherwise make r > g a fixed point rather than a drift; (3) the vacation of positions of intellectual authority permits paradigm turnover, an effect measured empirically in the literature on the premature death of eminent scientists; (4) willingness to accept mortality risk scales with remaining life-years and with wealth, so that the risk premium demanded for frontier activity rises without bound as both increase; and (5) exit from positions generates the vacancy chains through which career mobility occurs.

The paper further argues that artificial agents constitute the first economic actors with arbitrary, designer-specified lifespans, and that the turnover functions above may migrate to them, producing a permanent asset-holding human population alongside a mortal artificial workforce that bears risk and establishes presence on any frontier. Property doctrines that assign title on the basis of occupation, combined with communication latency that makes remote supervision physically impossible, suggest a principal-agent problem with historical precedent in the chartered trading companies.

The paper concludes that institutions performing these five functions must be constructed deliberately, that each takes the form of converting a perpetual claim into a renewable term, and that the window for adopting them closes when the affected parties can identify their own position, since mortality is the mechanism that currently enforces something like a Rawlsian veil of ignorance in institutional design.

detail.abstract: Recent advances in medicine and the rising costs of diagnostics and treatments have been increasing the pressure on healthcare systems lately. As a result, governments and private healthcare providers have been looking at ways to improve their performance. The use of network-DEA has been widely recognized in recent literature as one of the best benchmarking approaches for assessing performance, especially in hospital settings. However, this method cannot handle imperfectly known data. As an answer, this paper uses a novel network-Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) with a hit-and-run routine model applied to healthcare. Using this solution, hospital performance can be assessed even with imperfect data. Accordingly, data from 39 local healthcare units in Portugal reporting to 2024 were used as a case study, along with a framework divided into four subunits (eciency, inpatient, outpatient, and surgery). Furthermore, the integration with undesirable outputs, common in healthcare, was also achieved. The results suggest that medium-sized hospitals in Portugal exhibit the greatest ineciencies, particularly in outpatient services and the surgery department. Additionally, it was possible to conclude that the access dimension of healthcare is the least ecient, due to long waiting times. A sensitivity analysis comparing the hit-and-run procedure to the original network-DEA model was also performed. This comparison suggests that the proposed methodology is robust and can deal with missing data and potential data inaccuracies. It also revealed that the results obtained might be closer to reality than those from the network-DEA, providing stakeholders with more reliable information about the healthcare system's actual operations.

detail.abstract: That a performance metric distorts the behavior it monitors is well established (Kerr, 1975; Goodhart, 1975; Campbell, 1976; Hood, 2006; Ordonez, Schweitzer, Galinsky, & Bazerman, 2009). What this literature has not supplied is a principled account of why a given metric's distortion takes one specific shape rather than another: why some key performance indicators produce a narrow, surgical blind spot around one excluded relationship, while others produce a diffuse blindness with no clear excluded object at all. This paper argues that Learnable Theory's existing grammatical typology of attentional mechanisms, developed to distinguish how relators, nouns, and adjectives each background different content by different structural means, supplies exactly this missing account when applied to the linguistic form of the metric itself. A key performance indicator is not a neutral numerical instrument; it is a lexical construction with a specific grammatical profile, and that profile is argued to determine, structurally and in advance, the shape of the blind spot the metric will produce. The paper develops this typology across three metric forms, relational metrics (rates and ratios), threshold metrics (raw counts and totals), and composite metrics (weighted indices), and applies it to the Wells Fargo cross-selling scandal, showing that the bank's central metric, accounts opened per employee, was a relational construction predicting, before any fraud occurred, targeted exclusion of exactly the relationship, customer intent, that the metric never selected. The paper closes with a diagnostic procedure for classifying a proposed metric's grammatical type prior to deployment, extending Learnable Theory beyond its established domain of institutional language into the design of the measurement instruments institutions build to govern themselves.

detail.abstract: U.S. medical device small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)-roughly 80% of domestic manufacturers-face structural cost disadvantages rooted in channel partner economics, forecast-driven inventory management, and Group Purchasing Organization (GPO) contracting dynamics. This paper presents a two-track operational framework, grounded in field-tested practice, for addressing these disadvantages: (1) Channel Partner Building & Management (CPBM), a standardized process for evaluating and developing distributor performance, and (2) a Kanban-based, demand-driven inventory system that replaces forecast-driven replenishment with real-time consumption signals. Applied at a mid-sized medical device operating unit, the framework produced a 17.8% year-over-year revenue increase, a 67% reduction in lead time, and a 19.2% reduction in annual SG&A. The paper situates these firm-level results within the broader literature on supply chain resilience and B2B channel economics, and estimates the potential industry-wide impact of broader adoption across the approximately 5,000-firm U.S. medical device SME segment, including implications for domestic manufacturing employment and downstream healthcare procurement costs.

detail.abstract:
Frontline human-service organizations provide emergency relief, housing support, addiction recovery, post-incarceration reentry, and other assistance that markets cannot sustain on their own. Donations and grants remain indispensable, but systems organized around visible, countable, and time-bounded outputs can also shape what organizations learn to design. Across legal forms, employment initiatives often ask beadwork and other low-differentiation goods to perform four functions simultaneously: therapy, work-readiness training, market exchange, and mission finance. The first two may be real even when the latter two are absent.

This is a practice-grounded, agenda-setting conceptual article rather than a definitive empirical verdict. It draws on direct operation of a Chinese social enterprise beginning in 2009, longitudinal collaboration and repeated field observation in South Korea beginning in 2010, and the subsequent creation and operation of a U.S. 501(c)(3). Two practice laboratories anchor the analysis: Yilinquan, a differentiated corporate-lunch restaurant in Beijing, and The Up Korea, a cookie enterprise inside a long-standing addiction-recovery system. The Qicheng initiative illustrates how a high-value product system can be decomposed into progressive jobs.

Rather than restating the established proposition that nonprofits and mission-driven organizations may earn income, the article asks what kind of value produces that income and how operating contribution may be converted into participant-facing mission capacity. The proposed mechanism runs from independent market value to sustainable price premium and operating contribution, then to mission space, responsibility buffering, and potentially more stable social reintegration. Mission space is the financial, temporal, and decision capacity that can follow a person's actual constraints rather than a single restricted category. Responsibility buffering regulates the pace at which obligations return during transition from protected support to ordinary life.

The evidence is deliberately graded. The cases provide existence and front-end mechanism evidence for Propositions 1 and 2; Propositions 3 and 4 remain theoretical extensions requiring longitudinal and multi-site testing. The article contributes a four-value distinction, a value-creation mechanism positioned against earned-income and blended-value scholarship, a seven-layer design framework, and an open research agenda that invites independent verification, refinement, boundary setting, or rejection. It does not estimate average profitability or claim that the full sequence has already been causally demonstrated.

detail.title: Pensions and Turbulence: Automatic Adjustment, Risk, and Fairness in Long-Term Pension Design
detail.abstract: Public pension systems are long-term social contracts operating under persistent economic, demographic, and political uncertainty. Periods of turbulence, marked by financial shocks, changes in longevity, and shifting labour markets, test the capacity of pension institutions to adapt while maintaining adequacy, equity, and legitimacy. Building on earlier joint work on pension economics and reform with Nicholas Barr, this chapter analyses the role of automatic and semi-automatic adjustment mechanisms in public pension design. Drawing on comparative experience from Sweden, Canada, and the United States, we examine mechanisms for maintaining financial balance, the incorporation of life expectancy into retirement age and benefit design, and the accumulation and drawdown phases of defined contribution pensions. We argue that well-designed automatic mechanisms can discipline political decision-making and improve resilience, but only if they are proportionate, transparent, and attentive to distributional and intergenerational consequences. In turbulent times, good pension design does not eliminate the need for political choice; rather, it structures that choice so that adjustment can occur without repeated crises.

title: Modeling Supply-Chain and Transport Resilience to Climate Risks: Lessons from Four Regions
affiliations: International Institute of Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) and World Bank

detail.title: Modeling Supply-Chain and Transport Resilience to Climate Risks: Lessons from Four Regions
detail.abstract: Building resilience to natural hazards requires more than identifying critical assets. It requires understanding how supply chains respond to disruptions: where suppliers are located, what inventories firms hold, how diversified their sourcing is, and how products are transported. This paper summarizes key insights from DisruptSC, a spatial agent-based model that jointly represents the transport network and firm-level supply chains, applied to four countries or regions: Tanzania, Cambodia, Ecuador, and the Middle Corridor (Central Asia and South Caucasus). Five policy-relevant findings emerge. First, the duration of a disruption is a primary driver of total economic losses, making fast recovery a crucial lever for risk reduction. Second, the distribution of direct damages across firms and facilities matters as much as the total damages in determining total economic losses. Third, compounding events striking in close succession amplify losses in non-trivial ways, so that individual events cannot be assessed in isolation. Fourth, shorter supply chains do not always increase resilience: they buffer small, frequent disruptions but amplify large ones, reflecting a trade-off between efficiency and resilience that depends on the characteristics of the firm network and the nature of the risks. And fifth, resilience is a network externality—its benefits spill across firms and across borders — so markets under-provide it, and coordinated policy, within and between countries, has a role to play. The paper also illustrates how the model can be used for operational risk assessments or investment prioritization through transport investment stress testing, hotspot identification, and cost-benefit analyses that capture supply chain impacts.

title: Economic Preferences Predict Higher-Education Choices
affiliations: University of Lille, University of Zurich - Department of Economics, , University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Economic Preferences Predict Higher-Education Choices
detail.abstract: We examine whether individual preferences predict higher education choices. According to standard human capital theory, differences in individuals’ time and risk preferences lead to differences in educational investments. Testing this hypothesis is challenging, as it requires measuring individuals’ preferences, doing so before they make educational investments, and subsequently observing their educational choices. We combine incentivized, experimentally elicited measures of time and risk preferences for a large, representative sample of 18–19-year-old Danes with administrative data on subsequent higher education choices, program-specific earnings trajectories, prior school performance, and family background. In line with theory, we find that more patient individuals choose longer education programs and programs with steeper early-career earnings profiles, while more risk-averse individuals select programs with lower earnings dispersion and reduced downside risk. These relationships remain strong after controlling for cognitive ability, prior academic performance, and family background. Our findings suggest that preferences have a substantial impact on real-world educational investments and have implications for educational sorting.

title: A Model of Global Firms and Capital Markets
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis, Columbia University - Columbia Business School and University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Carlson School of Management

detail.title: A Model of Global Firms and Capital Markets
detail.abstract: We develop a general-equilibrium model of the global economy that integrates heterogeneous firms competing in product markets with countries that allocate capital around the world. Combining a hedonic demand system on the product side with a mean-variance portfolio system on the asset side, we obtain almost closed-form solutions for the equilibrium of the model. We use firm-level data on balance sheets, geographic breakdowns of revenue and employment, and business descriptions along with country-level data on bilateral equity holdings and trade costs to quantify the model to a cross section of roughly 23,000 listed firms in 48 countries. We use the model to evaluate the reallocation and welfare effects of globalization. Both financial and trade liberalization concentrate activity among the largest firms and raise welfare, with gains being larger in emerging and mid-sized open economies respectively. Product- and capital-market frictions amplify each other, meaning that liberalizing one market reduces the gains from liberalizing the other.

title: Carbon Taxation and Firm Behavior in Emerging Economies: Evidence from South Africa
affiliations: Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK), United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research (UNU-WIDER), National University Singapore, University of Münster and

detail.title: Carbon Taxation and Firm Behavior in Emerging Economies: Evidence from South Africa
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first comprehensive evidence on how firms in an emerging economy respond to carbon taxation in the context of an early-phase policy, highlighting how firms adjust when incentives are modest but signals about future regulation are strong. We study the announcement and early implementation of South Africa’s 2019 carbon tax using detailed administrative firm-level data from 2011-2021. Employing a matched difference-in-differences design and event-study models, we trace dynamic firm responses. Contrary to concerns that carbon taxes might hinder growth or employment, we find no negative effects on firm performance or jobs. Leveraging variation in firms’ exposure to the tax through temporary tax-free allowances, we find that firms facing higher effective tax rates increased sales, employment, capital, and capital depreciation in anticipation of the policy, reflecting resolution of regulatory uncertainty and adjustments to mitigate stranded asset risks. While we detect no measurable reduction in emissions — likely due to anticipatory behavior — the results show that early-phase carbon pricing can shape firm behavior without harming economic outcomes, even in low- and middle-income settings.

title: Industrial Policy and Capital Misallocation in Exporting
affiliations: , National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Finance, University of California, Berkeley and National University of Singapore - Department of Finance

detail.title: Industrial Policy and Capital Misallocation in Exporting

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Trade financing through export credit agencies is a key tool of modern industrial policy. We provide a theory to evaluate its welfare effects, and we study its causal impact on trade, firm investment, and capital misallocation by using the effective shutdown of the US export credit agency from 2015 to 2019 as a natural experiment. First, we show that the US Export-Import Bank (EXIM) has large causal effects: comparing industries exposed and unexposed to the shutdown, we find that exposed industries experience a product-level export reduction of approximately $4.49 for each $1 lost in EXIM financing. EXIM-dependent firms also experience substantial contractions in revenues, investment, and employment. Second, shutting down EXIM increases capital misallocation because firms with high marginal revenue product of capital (MRPK) disproportionately contract while low-MRPK firms are largely unaffected. Terms-of-trade adjustments and freeing capital for domestic producers do not appear to offset these losses empirically. Our results indicate that even in advanced economies with developed financial markets, industrial policy that lowers financing constraints for exporters can raise output, improve capital allocation, and generate welfare gains.
